glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 20 admits that no one can make his heart clean and sets every life before the LORD, who detests dishonest weights and directs each step, and whose lamp, the spirit of a man, searches the heart; the wise are called to stop striving, deal honestly, and wait for Him instead of repaying evil.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The sayings belong to Solomon’s collection begun at 10:1. Royal sayings run through the chapter (20:2, 8, 26, 28), and the warning against dishonest weights appears twice (20:10, 23).

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “The spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD, Searching all the inner depths of his heart.” (Proverbs 20:27)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 20 opens with the bottle and the brawl. “Wine is a mocker, Strong drink is a brawler” (20:1), as if drink itself had joined the scoffers. Against the noise of quarrels, “It is honorable for a man to stop striving” (20:3). Beneath it all lies the heart, where “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water” (20:5).

The chapter’s central question exposes that heart. No one can honestly say, “I have made my heart clean” (20:9), and the sayings around it are full of seeing eyes. The king scatters evil “with his eyes” (20:8), the LORD made “The hearing ear and the seeing eye” (20:12), and He calls diverse weights an abomination, a warning given twice (20:10, 23). Only God creates a clean heart (Psalm 51:10).

Two lamps mark the later sayings. The lamp of the one who curses his parents “will be put out in deep darkness” (20:20), but “The spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD” (20:27). Between them stand the call, “Wait for the LORD, and He will save you” (20:22), and the saying that “A man’s steps are of the LORD” (20:24). The God who directs each step also searches what lies within, and the chapter closes on blows that reach “the inner depths of the heart” (20:30).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 20:1–6 — Wine, Strife, and the Faithful Man

Drink stirs up trouble for the one it leads astray, provoking a king’s anger puts a man’s own life at risk, and stepping back from strife brings honor, since any fool can start a quarrel. The lazy man who will not plow because of winter begs at harvest and has nothing, and the closing pair sets the purposes a man of understanding draws out of the heart beside the many who proclaim their own goodness and the faithful man so hard to find.

Proverbs 20:7–12 — Who Can Say His Heart Is Clean?

A righteous man walks in integrity and his children are blessed after him, and a king on the throne of judgment scatters evil by his gaze. At the center, the question of 20:9 leaves every person without a claim to self-made purity, while the sayings around it show that the LORD detests double standards in trade, that even a child is known by his deeds, and that the ear and eye are His own work.

Proverbs 20:13–19 — Honest Dealing and Guarded Lips

Love of sleep leads to poverty while open eyes find bread, and the buyer who runs down the goods and then boasts of his bargain shows how easily small dishonesty slips into trade. Knowledgeable lips are worth more than gold and rubies, sweet bread won by deceit turns to gravel, plans need counsel, a pledge for a stranger is a poor risk, and neither the talebearer who reveals secrets nor the flatterer is a safe companion.

Proverbs 20:20–25 — Wait for the LORD

The one who curses father or mother has his lamp put out, an inheritance seized in haste is not blessed at the end, and the wronged man is told not to repay evil but to wait for the LORD to save him. Dishonest scales are condemned again, the LORD’s direction of a man’s steps puts his own way beyond his full understanding, and a vow made rashly becomes a snare.

Proverbs 20:26–30 — The King, the Lamp of the LORD, and Cleansing Blows

A wise king sifts the wicked like grain under the threshing wheel, yet mercy and truth preserve him and lovingkindness upholds his throne. The spirit of a man is the LORD’s lamp searching the heart’s inner depths, young strength and gray hair each have their glory, and blows that hurt cleanse away evil and reach the inner person, though the saying gives no license for abuse.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 20 keeps the righteous honest about themselves. The same chapter that praises the man who “walks in his integrity” (20:7) asks who can say his heart is clean (20:9). Righteousness in Proverbs is a way of life before God that includes humility and confession, and the cleansing no one can supply for himself comes from God, who forgives and cleanses those who confess (1 John 1:9).

The chapter also leaves vengeance with God. Personal revenge is ruled out, and the one who waits is promised that the LORD will save him (20:22; compare Romans 12:19); seeking lawful protection is not forbidden. The warning against dishonest scales stands right beside that promise (20:23), so the God who will right the wrongs done to His people also sees the quiet wrongs they might do in trade.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The heart and its depths. Counsel lies in the heart like deep water, no one can claim a heart made clean by his own effort, and both the LORD’s lamp and painful blows reach its inner depths (20:5, 9, 27, 30).

Honest dealing. Double weights and measures, the haggling buyer, and bread gained by deceit all fall under the LORD’s judgment of trade (20:10, 14, 17, 23).

Strife and revenge. Drink stirs up fights, provoking a king endangers a life, stepping back from a quarrel brings honor, and repaying evil is left to the LORD (20:1–3, 22).

The king and justice. The king’s wrath is fearsome and his gaze scatters evil, yet a wise king who sifts out the wicked is himself preserved by mercy and truth (20:2, 8, 26, 28).

Words and loyalty. Many proclaim their own goodness, lips of knowledge are a rare jewel, and the talebearer reveals secrets, so the flatterer is poor company (20:6, 15, 19).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Wine and strong drink (20:1). Pictured as a mocker and a brawler, drink deceives the one who trusts it and stirs up trouble. The verse warns against being “led astray by it,” and whoever is led astray “is not wise,” lacking the skill for living life God’s way; the full portrait comes in 23:29–35.

Diverse weights (20:10, 23). Two sets of weights or measures, one for buying and one for selling, so that the trader can cheat. An abomination is something the LORD finds detestable, and Proverbs sets dishonest scales against the just weight that is His delight (11:1).

Surety (20:16). Pledging oneself for another person’s debt. The saying tells the lender to take the garment of a man who guarantees a stranger’s debt and hold it as security, because such a man is a poor risk (compare 6:1–5).

Wait for the LORD (20:22). Trusting God to act on one’s behalf instead of taking personal revenge. The promise attached is “He will save you,” so the waiting rests on His faithfulness.

The lamp of the LORD (20:27). The spirit of a man, often understood as conscience and self-awareness, through which God brings to light what is hidden in a person. The exact sense of the phrase is debated; it refers to the human spirit, not the Holy Spirit, and it stands in contrast to the lamp put out in 20:20.

focus: Proverbs 20 gathers sayings on wine and strife, the heart no one can cleanse alone, honest dealing and guarded lips, waiting for the LORD rather than taking revenge, and the spirit of man as the lamp of the LORD.

sections.title: Wine, Strife, and the Faithful Man
sections.summary: Wine is a mocker and strong drink a brawler. It is honorable to stop striving, the lazy man will not plow, counsel in the heart is deep water, and a faithful man is hard to find.

sections.title: Who Can Say His Heart Is Clean?
sections.summary: The righteous man walks in integrity, and the king scatters evil with his eyes. No one can say he has made his heart clean, diverse weights are an abomination to the LORD, and the LORD has made the hearing ear and the seeing eye.

sections.title: Honest Dealing and Guarded Lips
sections.summary: The one who loves sleep comes to poverty. Lips of knowledge are a precious jewel, bread gained by deceit turns to gravel, plans are established by counsel, and the talebearer is to be avoided.

sections.title: Wait for the LORD
sections.summary: The one who curses his parents will have his lamp put out. The son must not say he will repay evil but wait for the LORD to save him, for a man’s steps are of the LORD, and rash vows are a snare.

sections.title: The King, the Lamp of the LORD, and Cleansing Blows
sections.summary: A wise king sifts out the wicked and is preserved by mercy and truth. The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching the inner depths, and blows that hurt cleanse away evil.

1.brief: Wine mocks and strong drink brawls, as if alcohol itself were a scoffer and a troublemaker, and whoever lets it lead him astray is not wise. The warning is against being carried off by drink, which deceives the one who trusts it and stirs up strife (compare 23:29–35).
1.explain:
“Wine is a mocker,”

The chapter opens by giving wine a character. It is “a mocker,” the same figure as the scoffer Proverbs warns against, the one who laughs at correction and sneers at what is right. Wine comes looking like a friend, but in the end it makes a fool of the one who trusts it, and it can turn the drinker himself into a mocker.

“Strong drink is a brawler,”

“Strong drink” is a brawler, noisy and quarrelsome. It stirs up trouble, loosens the tongue, and starts fights. The two lines personify alcohol as two of the troublemakers Proverbs describes most often, the scoffer and the man who loves strife.

“And whoever is led astray by it is not wise.”

The third line gives the verdict. Whoever is “led astray by it,” carried off, staggering, deceived into folly, “is not wise.” The warning is against being led astray by drink, letting it take control and lead a person where he would not go with a clear head. The verse warns against that loss of control; it does not lay down a further rule. Proverbs gives a much fuller portrait of the drunkard in 23:29–35, ending with wine that “bites like a serpent” (23:32), and Lemuel’s mother applies the warning to rulers in 31:4–5. The New Testament gives the same warning with its positive counterpart: “do not be drunk with wine, in which is dissipation; but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18).
1.notes: The KJV renders the second line ‘strong drink is raging,’ and it reads “deceived” where the NKJV has “led astray.” The NASB reads ‘whoever is intoxicated by it.’

2.brief: A king’s anger is as terrifying as a lion’s roar, and the one who provokes him puts his own life at risk. Following the brawler of verse 1, the saying warns that some quarrels are deadly, especially with those who hold power.
2.explain:
“The wrath of a king is like the roaring of a lion;”

The roar of a lion is a terrifying sound, and the “wrath of a king” is like that roar: terrifying, because the king holds the power of life and death. Proverbs used nearly the same picture in 19:12, and here it follows the brawler of 20:1. Some quarrels are far more dangerous than others.

“Whoever provokes him to anger sins against his own life.”

To provoke the king is to bring his anger on oneself, and the one who does it “sins against his own life.” He may think he is striking at the king’s pride, but the harm comes back on him. The verse calls this sin, not just foolishness: rash provocation of rightful authority wrongs one’s own life. The next verse draws the lesson for every kind of conflict: it is honorable to stop.

3.brief: It brings a man honor to step back from a fight, since any fool can start a quarrel. Real strength shows in ending strife; picking a fight takes no wisdom at all.
3.explain:
“It is honorable for a man to stop striving,”

“Honorable” here means bringing glory or credit. It is to a man’s honor “to stop striving,” to step back from a quarrel, to sit apart from strife. The world often counts backing down as weakness, but Proverbs calls it honor. Real strength shows itself in ending a conflict.

“Since any fool can start a quarrel.”

The reason is simple: “any fool can start a quarrel.” Picking a fight takes no wisdom, skill, or courage at all. Anyone can do it. Ending strife, or never starting it, takes self-control, humility, and a willingness to let one’s pride go unsatisfied. Following the warnings about the brawling drink of 20:1 and the provoked king of 20:2, this saying gives the wise response to conflict. It echoes 17:14, which urged stopping contention before a quarrel starts.
3.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “start a quarrel” describes a dispute breaking out into the open. It occurs only three times in the Old Testament, all in Proverbs: here, in 17:14 (“before a quarrel starts”), and in 18:1 (“rages against”). Each time it pictures conflict bursting out, which is what the fool is quick to start and the honorable man refuses to continue.

4.brief: The lazy man will not plow when the cold season comes, so at harvest time he looks for a crop and finds nothing. Excuses at planting time lead to emptiness at reaping time, and he ends up begging.
4.explain:
“The lazy man will not plow because of winter;”

In Israel, plowing and sowing were done in the cooler, wetter months, after the early rains softened the ground. That season could be cold and unpleasant. The lazy man uses it as his excuse: he “will not plow because of winter.” The discomfort is real, but it does not cancel the work. Waiting for comfortable conditions means the work never gets done.

“He will beg during harvest and have nothing.”

The consequence comes months later. When harvest arrives, he “will beg,” looking for a crop or asking others for food, and he will “have nothing.” Nothing grows where nothing was planted. The empty harvest is not bad luck; it is the fruit of the skipped season. Proverbs elsewhere gives a full portrait of the lazy man, and this saying shows his excuse and its end. It concerns a person able to work who refuses because the work is unpleasant. It says nothing against those prevented from working by illness, inability, or real hardship.
4.notes: The Hebrew word rendered “winter” refers to the autumn and winter season, the time after the early rains when the ground was plowed. The ESV reads ‘in the autumn,’ and the KJV text reads ‘by reason of the cold,’ with a margin reading “winter.”

5.brief: The purposes in a person’s heart are like water deep in a well, hidden from view, but a man of understanding knows how to draw them out. Wisdom includes the patient skill of listening and asking until what lies beneath comes to the surface.
5.explain:
“Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water,”

“Counsel” here means purpose or plan, the intentions and thoughts a person carries inside. They are “like deep water,” lying far below the surface in a well, hidden from view. People carry much more than they say. Their real purposes, fears, and understanding often lie deep.

“But a man of understanding will draw it out.”

“A man of understanding will draw it out,” as someone draws water from a deep well with a bucket and rope. He does not force or drill; he listens, asks, and waits patiently until what lies beneath comes to the surface. This is part of wisdom: the skill of understanding people, helping them bring their thoughts into the open, and discerning what is really going on. The verse applies to counselors, parents, friends, and leaders, and also to the wise person drawing out the counsel of quiet people who know more than they say. Proverbs used the image of deep waters for words in 18:4.
5.notes: The ESV renders “counsel” as ‘purpose’ and the NASB as ‘A plan,’ which brings out the sense of hidden intentions.

6.brief: Plenty of people will announce their own goodness and loyalty, but a truly faithful man is hard to find. Talk of kindness is cheap; steady faithfulness is rare and precious.
6.explain:
“Most men will proclaim each his own goodness,”

The Hebrew word behind “goodness” is chesed, loyal, faithful love. Many people “proclaim” their own goodness, announcing how loyal, kind, and dependable they are. Talk of such love is easy and common.

“But who can find a faithful man?”

The question exposes the gap between talk and reality. “Who can find a faithful man,” someone who actually proves dependable over time? Such a person is rare. Faithfulness is proved in action, not proclaimed in words, and many who announce their loyalty do not keep it when it costs them. The verse does not deny that faithful people exist; it says they are hard to find and precious when found. The same kind of question will be asked in 31:10 about the virtuous wife, and here it is asked about the faithful man. The question invites the reader to be the kind of person whose faithfulness others can find rather than only claim it.
6.notes: The ESV renders the first line ‘Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love,’ showing that the Hebrew word behind “goodness” is chesed, the word for loyal love. That word makes the contrast with the “faithful man” of the second line sharper: many claim loyal love, but few prove faithful.

7.brief: The righteous man lives with integrity, and his children are blessed after him. A godly life leaves an inheritance of example and blessing that reaches the next generation, as a general pattern of God’s ways.
7.explain:
“The righteous man walks in his integrity;”

The righteous man “walks in his integrity,” living with wholeness and honesty day after day. As in 19:1, integrity is a walk, the steady course of a life. His righteousness is not a claim to sinlessness; it is a way of life before God that includes humility and turning from sin when he fails.

“His children are blessed after him.”

The effect of his life reaches beyond him: “His children are blessed after him.” A godly life leaves an inheritance of example, reputation, and blessing that reaches the next generation. Children who grow up seeing integrity lived out receive something of great worth. This describes the general pattern of God’s ways, not a guarantee that every child of a righteous parent will prosper or follow the Lord, and it gives no ground for blaming parents whose children turn away. It says that a faithful walk today matters beyond one’s own lifetime.

8.brief: When a king sits on his judgment seat, his searching gaze scatters evil like chaff. A just ruler’s attention alone makes wrongdoers scatter, because they know he sees.
8.explain:
“A king who sits on the throne of judgment”

The verse pictures a king seated to hear cases, exercising his role as judge. In Israel the king was the highest court of appeal, and his attention to justice set the moral tone of the whole kingdom.

“Scatters all evil with his eyes.”

The king “scatters all evil with his eyes.” The Hebrew verb behind “scatters” is the verb for winnowing, tossing grain into the wind so that the chaff blows away. The just king’s searching, discerning look sees through the schemes of wrongdoers and brings their evil into the open, so that it cannot hide before his judgment seat. What the king discerns, he can then judge justly. Under a just ruler, the righteous have nothing to fear and evil cannot hold its ground. The next verse turns from the king’s gaze to a deeper question: if a just king’s eyes expose evil, who can stand before the eyes of God and claim a clean heart?
8.notes: The Hebrew verb rendered “scatters” means to scatter or to winnow, and it appears again in 20:26, where the wise king “sifts out the wicked.” The ESV reads “winnows” in both verses, which keeps the farming picture of separating chaff from grain.

9.brief: Who can honestly claim to have made his own heart clean and to be free from sin? The question expects the answer no one, for no person can purify himself; that need is met only by God, who creates a clean heart and cleanses those who confess (Psalm 51:10; 1 John 1:9).
9.explain:
“Who can say, ‘I have made my heart clean,’”

The verse is a question that expects the answer “no one.” Who can honestly say, “I have made my heart clean”? The claim is not merely that the heart is clean, but that the person made it so by his own effort. No human being can do this. The heart, the inner person, carries sin that no amount of self-improvement can remove.

“‘I am pure from my sin’?”

The second part of the claim goes further: “I am pure from my sin.” No one can say this truthfully. The question exposes the pride that would claim self-made purity and the honesty that admits the need for cleansing. This does not mean that the righteous of Proverbs are hypocrites. Their righteousness is real, but it is a way of life before God that includes humility and confession. As 28:13 puts it, “whoever confesses and forsakes them will have mercy” (28:13). The question prepares for the answer Scripture gives elsewhere. What no one can do for himself, God does. David prayed, “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10), and the New Testament promises, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Cleansing comes from God, not from the self.
9.notes: The verse stands right after the king who scatters evil with his eyes in 20:8, and just before the false weights of 20:10, so the question of the clean heart sits between royal justice and everyday honesty.

10.brief: Two sets of weights and two sets of measures, one for buying and one for selling, are equally detestable to the LORD. Cheating in trade is not a small matter of business; it offends the God who sees every transaction (compare 11:1).
10.explain:
“Diverse weights and diverse measures,”

Trade in Israel used stone weights in a balance and standard containers for measuring grain. “Diverse weights and diverse measures” means two sets of each, one heavy and one light, one large and one small. A dishonest merchant would use the heavy weight when buying and the light one when selling, cheating in both directions. The law forbade it plainly: “You shall not have in your bag differing weights, a heavy and a light” (Deuteronomy 25:13).

“They are both alike, an abomination to the LORD.”

Both the false weights and the false measures “are both alike, an abomination to the LORD.” He finds them detestable. Cheating in trade is not a small matter of business practice; it offends the God who sees every transaction. Proverbs already said, “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, But a just weight is His delight” (11:1). The doubleness itself is the sin: one standard for oneself and another for others. The saying returns almost word for word in 20:23. Placed right after the question of 20:9, it shows that the heart no one can cleanse alone reveals itself in such small, everyday dishonesty.
10.notes: The Hebrew is literally ‘a stone and a stone, an ephah and an ephah.’ The stone was a weight used in a balance, and an ephah was a standard dry measure for grain. The doubled words describe two different weights and two different measures used for the same purpose.

11.brief: Even a child shows by what he does whether his conduct is pure and right. Character shows itself early in actions, so behavior, not claims, reveals what is in the heart.
11.explain:
“Even a child is known by his deeds,”

“Even a child,” a young person, “is known by his deeds.” Character shows itself early. A child’s actions reveal what kind of person he is becoming, long before he is grown. Behavior, not claims, reveals what is in the heart.

“Whether what he does is pure and right.”

His deeds show “whether what he does is pure and right.” Even in childhood, conduct can be clean and upright or not. The saying takes the young seriously. What children do matters, and it already shows who they are becoming. Coming right after the question of 20:9, which no one can answer with a self-made clean heart, the verse also shows that the call to pure and right conduct remains. Knowing that only God can cleanse the heart does not cancel the call to live purely.
11.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “is known” is a form of the verb to recognize, and the ESV and YLT render it ‘makes himself known.’ The same verb form can elsewhere mean to disguise oneself, so the line may also hint that a child can mask his character for a time. The main versions follow the sense of being recognized by conduct.

12.brief: The ear that hears and the eye that sees were both made by the LORD. Since He gave these faculties, He hears and sees all things Himself, and people are accountable to use their ears and eyes as He intends.
12.explain:
“The hearing ear and the seeing eye,”

The verse names two faculties: “the hearing ear and the seeing eye.” In Proverbs the hearing ear is often the listening ear, the one that receives instruction, and the seeing eye perceives what is true. These are the senses through which a person takes in wisdom.

“The LORD has made them both.”

“The LORD has made them both.” Ears and eyes are His gifts and His design. Two truths follow. First, the God who made the ear hears, and the God who made the eye sees; nothing escapes Him. Second, people are accountable to use their ears and eyes as He intended, to listen to wisdom and to see rightly. The verse follows sayings about dishonest weights and a child’s deeds, where hidden things are exposed, and it reminds the reader that all of life is lived before the One who sees and hears everything. It prepares for the next verse, which tells the reader to open his eyes.

13.brief: Do not love sleep, or poverty will follow; keep your eyes open and you will have enough bread. The command sets drowsy self-indulgence against alert diligence, and each brings its own result.
13.explain:
“Do not love sleep, lest you come to poverty;”

The command is not “do not sleep.” Rest is God’s good gift. The warning is against loving sleep, making comfort and ease a person’s settled desire. The one who loves sleep comes “to poverty.” Drowsy self-indulgence that puts rest ahead of responsibility leads to want.

“Open your eyes, and you will be satisfied with bread.”

The opposite is to “open your eyes,” to stay awake, alert, and ready to work. The one who does “will be satisfied with bread,” having enough to eat. The command follows directly after 20:12, where the LORD made the seeing eye; here the reader is told to open it. Diligence is partly waking up to what God has already given and using it. Like other proverbs about work, this describes the general pattern of God’s world. Poverty has many causes besides laziness, and this saying does not blame every poor person for loving sleep.

14.brief: The buyer complains that the goods are worthless, then walks away and brags about the bargain he got. With a touch of humor, the proverb exposes the small dishonesty of haggling that runs down a product only to win a better price.
14.explain:
“‘It is good for nothing,’ cries the buyer;”

The scene is a market. The buyer examines the goods and complains loudly: “It is good for nothing.” He runs down the item, pointing out every flaw, hoping to drive the price down.

“But when he has gone his way, then he boasts.”

Once the deal is done and he “has gone his way,” the buyer “boasts” about the fine bargain he got. The thing he called worthless was worth much more than he paid. With a touch of humor, the proverb exposes the small dishonesty of haggling that uses words as tools rather than truth. His complaint was a pose, and his boasting shows what he really thought. The verse sits among sayings about honest trade and guarded speech, and it shows that dishonesty can hide even in ordinary bargaining.
14.notes: In Hebrew the buyer’s complaint is the word for “bad” said twice, ‘Bad, bad,’ as the ESV and NASB render it.

15.brief: Gold and many rubies exist, but lips that speak with knowledge are a rarer jewel. Wise speech is worth more than wealth because it is harder to find and does more good.
15.explain:
“There is gold and a multitude of rubies,”

The verse opens almost casually: “There is gold and a multitude of rubies.” Gold and precious stones exist in the world, and people can find and own them. They are valuable, but they are not rare in the sense the next line means.

“But the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel.”

What is truly rare is “the lips of knowledge,” speech that comes from real understanding. Such lips are “a precious jewel,” worth more than gold and rubies because they are harder to find and do more good. A person who speaks true knowledge, wisely and at the right time, is a treasure. Wise speech can guide, warn, comfort, and teach in ways no amount of wealth can. In a section about honest dealing and guarded lips, this verse sets the value of wise words above material riches.
15.notes: The Hebrew phrase behind “precious jewel” is literally ‘a vessel of preciousness,’ an object of great value, and the YLT renders it ‘a precious vessel.’ After the gold and rubies of the first line, the wording sets wise speech among a person’s treasured possessions, something to be valued and kept.

16.brief: A lender should take the garment of anyone who guarantees a stranger’s debt and hold it as security when he has pledged on behalf of a seductress. A man that careless is a poor risk, so the saying warns, with dry realism, against rash surety (compare 6:1–5).
16.explain:
“Take the garment of one who is surety for a stranger,”

The saying speaks to a lender. If a man becomes “surety for a stranger,” guaranteeing the debt of someone he does not know, the lender should “take the garment” of the guarantor as security. A man who pledges for strangers is careless with his commitments, and the lender is wise to protect himself. Proverbs has warned the guarantor before, in 6:1–5, 11:15 and 17:18; here the warning comes from the lender’s side.

“And hold it as a pledge when it is for a seductress.”

If the guarantor has pledged on behalf of “a seductress,” an immoral woman, he is an even poorer risk. A man that rash with his commitments and his company cannot be trusted to pay, so the lender should hold the pledge firmly. The saying is dry and realistic. It warns against rash surety by showing how others will see it, and it implies that a person known for careless pledges loses the trust of those who deal with him. The law also limited such pledges with mercy, requiring a garment taken in pledge to be returned before sunset, as Exodus 22:26 directs. The saying warns against rash pledges; it does not forbid all help to others.
16.notes:
This verse is repeated almost exactly at 27:13.

The Hebrew text has two readings in the second line. The written text has ‘foreigners,’ while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts has ‘a foreign woman.’ The NKJV and KJV follow the marginal reading, and the ESV and NASB follow the written text. At 27:13, where the saying is repeated, the Hebrew has only the feminine form, and the NKJV reads “seductress” there as well.

17.brief: Bread gained by deceit tastes sweet at first, but afterward the mouth is filled with gravel. Dishonest gain delights for a moment and then turns bitter and painful.
17.explain:
“Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man,”

Gain by dishonesty tastes good at first. “Bread gained by deceit,” food or income obtained through lying or cheating, “is sweet to a man.” The pleasure is real, and part of what makes deceit tempting is that it often works for a while.

“But afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel.”

The second line turns on the word “afterward.” The same mouth that tasted sweetness will be “filled with gravel,” grit that breaks the teeth and fills the mouth with pain. Dishonest gain delights for a moment and then turns bitter. The verse teaches that choices must be judged by their end, not their first taste. Its picture recalls Folly’s invitation in chapter 9, where “bread eaten in secret is pleasant” (9:17) but leads to death. Proverbs consistently weighs the pleasure of sin against its outcome.

18.brief: Plans succeed through counsel, and even war should be waged with wise guidance. The larger the stakes, the more a person needs the advice of others before acting.
18.explain:
“Plans are established by counsel;”

Plans become firm, “established,” through “counsel,” the advice of others. A person who plans alone, without seeking the wisdom of others, is more likely to fail. Wise planning includes listening, asking, and weighing the input of those who see what we may miss. Proverbs repeatedly praises counsel, and here it ties success in planning to it.

“By wise counsel wage war.”

The second line raises the stakes. Even war, the most serious undertaking of a nation, should be waged “by wise counsel.” The larger the stakes, the more a person needs the guidance of others before acting. The same counsel appears in 24:6: “For by wise counsel you will wage your own war” (24:6). The verse follows the warning about deceit in 20:17 and precedes the warning about gossips in 20:19, and it points to the kind of advisers worth having: wise, trustworthy, and discreet.
18.notes: The Hebrew word rendered “wise counsel” in the second line means guidance or direction. It is the word used in 1:5 and 24:6, where it describes the skilled guidance a wise person acquires and a nation needs in war.

19.brief: The gossip goes around revealing secrets, so do not keep company with someone whose lips flatter. The one who flatters you to your face will likely carry your private matters to others.
19.explain:
“He who goes about as a talebearer reveals secrets;”

A “talebearer” is a gossip, someone who “goes about” from person to person, carrying stories. He “reveals secrets,” passing on what was told to him in confidence. Proverbs has described the talebearer before, in 11:13 and 18:8, and here it adds a practical conclusion.

“Therefore do not associate with one who flatters with his lips.”

“Therefore” draws the lesson: “do not associate with one who flatters with his lips.” The flatterer and the talebearer are often the same person. He pleases you with smooth words so that you will tell him more, and then he carries what you said to others. The one who gossips to you will gossip about you. The verse calls for wisdom in choosing close companions. It does not call for suspicion of everyone, but it does warn against keeping company with a loose talker who cannot keep a confidence. In a section about counsel and honest speech, this saying shows who should not be trusted with one’s plans.
19.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “one who flatters with his lips” can be connected with a verb meaning to open wide, so the phrase may describe one who opens his lips wide, a loose talker. A verb of the same spelling means to entice or deceive, which lies behind the NKJV’s “flatters” and the KJV margin’s ‘enticeth.’ The ESV reads ‘a simple babbler.’

20.brief: Whoever curses father or mother will have his lamp put out in deep darkness. Despising one’s parents leads to the snuffing out of life and hope, the opposite of the long life promised to those who honor them (Exodus 20:12).
20.explain:
“Whoever curses his father or his mother,”

To “curse” one’s father or mother is to speak against them with contempt, to wish them harm, or to treat them as worthless. It is the direct opposite of the command to honor them. The law treated it with the utmost seriousness: “And he who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death” (Exodus 21:17).

“His lamp will be put out in deep darkness.”

A “lamp” in Proverbs stands for life, prosperity, and hope. For the one who curses his parents, “His lamp will be put out in deep darkness.” His life and future are snuffed out, leaving him in blackness. The picture is the opposite of the long life promised in Exodus 20:12 to those who honor their parents. The verse states the general consequence of despising one’s parents, a theme Proverbs returns to often. It begins a section in which the son is warned about grasping, about revenge, and about rash vows, and it sets honor for parents at the start of that instruction.
20.notes: The phrase rendered “deep darkness” is unusual. The Hebrew says literally ‘the pupil of darkness,’ an expression for the blackest middle of the night. Versions render it in different ways: the ESV “utter darkness,” the YLT ‘blackness of darkness,’ and the NASB ‘in time of darkness.’

21.brief: An inheritance seized in haste at the beginning will not be blessed at the end. Wealth grabbed through impatience or grasping, coming right after the warning about cursing parents in verse 20, lacks the blessing that comes with patient, honest receiving.
21.explain:
“An inheritance gained hastily at the beginning”

An “inheritance” is property passed down in a family. This one is “gained hastily at the beginning,” grabbed too soon, before its time, through impatience or grasping. The verse follows the warning about cursing parents, and it may picture a son who seizes his inheritance early, pressing or even pushing aside his parents to get it.

“Will not be blessed at the end.”

Such an inheritance “will not be blessed at the end.” What looks like early gain turns into late loss. Wealth grabbed through impatience lacks the blessing that comes with patient, honest receiving. The verse judges by the end, as Proverbs often does. It does not say that every early inheritance is cursed, and it does not describe those who receive an inheritance early through no grasping of their own. It warns against the hasty grab that dishonors both parents and God’s timing.
21.notes: The Hebrew text has two readings of one word here. The written text has a word meaning gained by greed, while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts means hurried or hastened. The NKJV, ESV and NASB follow the marginal reading, “hastily” or its equivalent. The YLT’s ‘An inheritance gotten wrongly at first’ appears to reflect the written reading.

22.brief: Do not say you will pay back evil for evil; wait for the LORD, and He will deliver you. Personal revenge is ruled out, and the wronged person entrusts justice to God (compare Romans 12:19), though this does not forbid seeking lawful protection.
22.explain:
“Do not say, ‘I will recompense evil’;”

The verse begins with speech. “Do not say, ‘I will recompense evil.’” Revenge begins as a sentence a person says to himself, a vow to pay back the wrong done to him. The command forbids that vow. Personal revenge is ruled out. Proverbs gives the same command elsewhere: “Do not say, ‘I will do to him just as he has done to me’” (24:29).

“Wait for the LORD, and He will save you.”

Instead, the wronged person is told to “wait for the LORD.” Waiting is not passive; it is active hope that holds on to God and trusts Him to act. The promise is “He will save you,” deliverance for the one wronged, rather than a description of the enemy’s punishment. What a wounded heart needs most is rescue, and God promises it. The New Testament carries the same teaching: “do not avenge yourselves, but rather give place to wrath; for it is written, ‘Vengeance is Mine, I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Romans 12:19). Waiting for the LORD does not forbid seeking lawful justice or protection. A person wronged may report a crime, seek help from authorities, or protect himself and others from harm. What is forbidden is taking personal vengeance.
22.notes: Paul’s words in Romans 12:19 quote Deuteronomy 32:35, “Vengeance is Mine, and recompense” (Deuteronomy 32:35), rather than this proverb, though the teaching is closely related.

23.brief: Unequal weights are detestable to the LORD, and crooked scales are not good. Repeating verse 10, the saying stands beside the call to wait for the LORD, as if to say that the God who will right wrongs also hates the quiet theft of dishonest trade.
23.explain:
“Diverse weights are an abomination to the LORD,”

The saying of 20:10 returns in a slightly different form. “Diverse weights,” two sets of stones for the scale, “are an abomination to the LORD.” He finds them detestable. Proverbs repeats this teaching because the temptation to cheat in small ways is constant and common.

“And dishonest scales are not good.”

“Dishonest scales are not good,” a mild understatement that leaves the reader to feel the weight. The saying stands between “Wait for the LORD” in 20:22 and “A man’s steps are of the LORD” in 20:24. Placed there, it suggests that honesty is a form of trust. The person who believes the LORD will defend him and guide his steps does not need to tip the scale in his own favor. The God who will right the wrongs done to His people also hates the quiet theft of dishonest trade.
23.notes: The law required one honest standard: “You shall have honest scales, honest weights” (Leviticus 19:36).

24.brief: A man’s steps are directed by the LORD, so how can anyone fully understand his own way? Human beings walk a path God oversees, which is why they must trust Him instead of relying on their own understanding (compare 16:9).
24.explain:
“A man’s steps are of the LORD;”

A person’s “steps,” the actual course of his life, “are of the LORD.” God directs and oversees them. This repeats the teaching of 16:9: “A man’s heart plans his way, But the LORD directs his steps” (16:9). Human beings make choices, and those choices matter, yet the LORD is sovereign over the path.

“How then can a man understand his own way?”

If God directs the steps, “how then can a man understand his own way?” No one can see the whole map of his life. People often understand God’s leading only looking back, and sometimes not even then. The question is not a call to fatalism or to stop thinking and planning. It calls for trust. Since no one can fully understand his own way, he must rely on the One who directs it, as 3:5–6 urges: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, And lean not on your own understanding” (3:5). Not understanding is not failure; it is the normal condition of a creature walking with his Creator.
24.notes: Jeremiah expresses the same truth: “It is not in man who walks to direct his own steps” (Jeremiah 10:23).

25.brief: It is a trap for a person to rashly declare something holy to God and only afterward think through what he has vowed. Promises to God are serious, so they should be weighed before they are made, not regretted after (compare Ecclesiastes 5:4–5).
25.explain:
“It is a snare for a man to devote rashly something as holy,”

To “devote rashly something as holy” is to declare suddenly that something belongs to God, dedicating money, property, or an offering to Him in a burst of enthusiasm, without thinking it through. Such a vow becomes a “snare,” a trap that catches the one who made it.

“And afterward to reconsider his vows.”

Only “afterward” does he “reconsider his vows,” beginning to think about what he has promised and perhaps wishing he had not. By then he is bound. A vow to God is serious, and breaking it is sin: “When you make a vow to God, do not delay to pay it” (Ecclesiastes 5:4). The verse calls for thought before commitment. It is not meant to make people afraid of making promises to God. Thoughtful devotion is no less devoted than impulsive devotion, and a commitment carefully weighed is more likely to be kept. The warning applies to every serious promise made to God.
25.notes: The Hebrew verb in the first line can mean to speak rashly or to swallow. The ESV and NASB take the first sense and render the line as saying rashly, ‘It is holy.’ The KJV takes the second and reads ‘devoureth that which is holy.’

26.brief: A wise king separates out the wicked as a farmer threshes grain, driving the threshing wheel over them. Like the king of verse 8, the just ruler does not leave evil mixed in with good but removes it from his realm.
26.explain:
“A wise king sifts out the wicked,”

A “wise king sifts out the wicked,” separating them from the righteous as a farmer winnows grain, tossing it into the wind so that the chaff blows away. This repeats the picture of 20:8, where the king scatters evil with his eyes. Here the image is stronger: the wise king actively removes the wicked from his realm.

“And brings the threshing wheel over them.”

The second line pictures threshing. A heavy wheel or sledge was driven over harvested grain to break the husks from the kernels. The king “brings the threshing wheel over them,” dealing firmly with the wicked so that evil does not stay mixed in with good. Wisdom is not softness toward evil. Protecting the good sometimes means removing what destroys it. The verse speaks of a king’s responsibility to deal justly with the wicked, and the next sayings balance this firmness: the lamp of the LORD searches the heart, and the king’s throne rests on mercy and truth.

27.brief: The spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD, searching out the inner rooms of the heart. God uses the human spirit, often understood as conscience and self-awareness, to bring to light what is hidden inside a person; this is the human spirit, not the Holy Spirit.
27.explain:
“The spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD,”

“The spirit of a man” is the breath of life God placed in human beings, the inner self with its awareness and conscience. That spirit is “the lamp of the LORD,” a light God uses to search and show a person what is within. The human spirit, often understood as conscience and self-awareness, is His instrument. This is the human spirit, not the Holy Spirit. The verse speaks of what God has placed in every person, not of the Spirit of God who indwells believers.

“Searching all the inner depths of his heart.”

The lamp is “searching all the inner depths of his heart,” shining into the hidden rooms of a person’s inner life. A lamp searches by showing, bringing to light what was hidden in darkness. God uses the human conscience to reveal motives, desires, and sins a person might prefer not to see. This searching is meant to reveal so that God can heal and correct, not to frighten. Paul similarly speaks of “the spirit of the man which is in him” (1 Corinthians 2:11) as knowing a person’s own thoughts. In a section about the king’s searching justice, this verse shows that God searches far deeper than any king can.
27.notes:
The Hebrew word for “spirit” here is neshamah, “breath.” It is the word used in Genesis 2:7, where God “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7), so the verse ties the lamp of the LORD to the life God Himself breathed into human beings.

The Hebrew phrase behind “inner depths” is literally ‘chambers of the belly,’ a picture of a person’s hidden inner life. It is the same phrase that lies behind “inmost body” in 18:8 and “inner depths” in 20:30.

The first line has no verb in Hebrew. It sets ‘the lamp of the LORD’ beside ‘the breath of man,’ and the NKJV, ESV, NASB and KJV supply “is,” identifying the human spirit as the LORD’s lamp.

28.brief: Mercy and truth guard the king, and by faithful love he holds his throne steady. After the stern justice of verse 26, the saying shows that a ruler’s throne finally rests on kindness and faithfulness.
28.explain:
“Mercy and truth preserve the king,”

Two qualities guard a king: “Mercy,” loyal, faithful love, and “truth,” faithfulness and reliability. They “preserve the king,” protecting him and his rule. A king surrounded by soldiers may still fall, but a king whose rule is marked by mercy and truth has a deeper security.

“And by lovingkindness he upholds his throne.”

The second line repeats “lovingkindness,” the same Hebrew word, chesed, as “mercy” in the first line. By that faithful love, “he upholds his throne,” holding it steady. After the stern justice of 20:26, where the wise king threshes the wicked, this verse shows that a ruler’s throne finally rests on kindness and faithfulness. Justice and mercy belong together. True authority is secured by love and truth, not by hardness alone. Proverbs elsewhere says, “a throne is established by righteousness” (16:12), and here mercy and truth stand beside righteousness as the foundations of good rule.
28.notes: The ESV renders the word as “steadfast love” in both lines, showing that the same Hebrew word stands behind the NKJV’s “Mercy” and “lovingkindness.”

29.brief: Young men take pride in their strength, and old men wear gray hair as their splendor. Each stage of life has its own honor, the vigor of youth and the wisdom and dignity of age.
29.explain:
“The glory of young men is their strength,”

Young men take pride in “their strength,” the energy, vigor, and endurance of youth. It is their glory, the honor that belongs to their stage of life. Strength is a good gift, not the source of a young man’s worth, and youth is the time it is at its peak.

“And the splendor of old men is their gray head.”

Old men have a different glory: “their gray head.” Gray hair is their “splendor,” a mark of long life, experience, and the wisdom that should come with age. Proverbs elsewhere says, “The silver-haired head is a crown of glory, If it is found in the way of righteousness” (16:31). Each stage of life has its own honor. The verse does not set young against old in competition; it shows that both have something to give. God’s people need the strength of the young and the wisdom of the old together.

30.brief: Blows that wound clean away evil, and strokes reach the inner depths of the heart. Painful correction can do what words alone may not, reaching and changing the inner person, though the verse gives no license for abuse or harsh punishment.
30.explain:
“Blows that hurt cleanse away evil,”

“Blows that hurt,” painful wounds and strokes, “cleanse away evil.” The verse speaks of correction, discipline that causes pain in order to remove wrongdoing. Painful correction can do what words alone sometimes cannot. It can break the hold of a sinful pattern and bring a person to his senses.

“As do stripes the inner depths of the heart.”

“Stripes,” strokes of correction, reach “the inner depths of the heart.” The Hebrew phrase behind “inner depths” is the same one used in 20:27, where the LORD’s lamp searches the inner depths. The place God’s lamp searches is the place His correction reaches. The goal is inner change, cleansing the heart, not merely punishing the body. The verse does not justify abuse or harsh punishment of children or anyone else. In Proverbs, discipline is the whole work of teaching, guiding, correcting, and training, and correction serves restoration. It must never be an outlet for anger, cruelty, or humiliation. God’s own discipline aims at good: “afterward it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11). The verse states that painful correction can reach and change the inner person, and it leaves the manner of correction to be governed by love.
30.notes: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult. In the first line the written text has a verb meaning to scour or polish, while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts has a related noun meaning a scouring or remedy. The KJV reads ‘The blueness of a wound cleanseth away evil,’ and its margin, ‘is a purging medicine against,’ reflects the noun. The YLT takes the word as a verb addressed to the reader, ‘thou removest,’ which produces a quite different sentence. The NKJV, ESV, NASB and AMP agree on the main sense of painful correction that cleanses.
